module_title: General Defenses & Mental Elements in Tort
introduction: This intermediate tier explores 'General Defenses'—the legal shields a defendant can use to avoid liability even if they committed the wrongful act. It also examines the irrelevance of motive in tort law.

core_concepts.title: Volenti Non Fit Injuria (Defense of Consent)
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'To a willing person, injury is not done.' 
- Rule: If a plaintiff voluntarily agrees to suffer harm, they cannot later sue for it (e.g., getting injured while playing a boxing match or attending a legal car race).
- Conditions: The consent must be free, and the act must be lawful.
- The Rescue Cases Exception: *Volenti* does NOT apply if the plaintiff is injured while acting under a legal or moral duty to rescue someone from a danger created by the defendant (*Haynes v. Harwood* - police officer stopping runaway horses).

core_concepts.title: Act of God (Vis Major)
core_concepts.description:
An extraordinary occurrence of circumstances that could not have been foreseen or prevented by any amount of human care and skill. 
- Conditions: (1) Must result from natural forces (heavy rainfall, earthquake), and (2) Must be extraordinarily unpredictable. 
- Landmark Case: *Nichols v. Marsland* - Exceptional rainfall broke the defendant's artificial lakes, flooding the plaintiff's bridges. Held to be an Act of God.

core_concepts.title: Inevitable Accident vs. Act of God
core_concepts.description:
- Inevitable Accident: An accident that could not have been avoided by ordinary care and skill, but may involve human agency (e.g., a tire bursting unexpectedly despite proper maintenance). 
- Act of God: Strictly involves natural forces with zero human intervention. All Acts of God are inevitable accidents, but not all inevitable accidents are Acts of God.

core_concepts.title: Private Defense & Statutory Authority
core_concepts.description:
- Private Defense: Use of reasonable and proportionate force to protect one's person or property against an imminent threat.
- Statutory Authority: If an act is authorized by a statute (like the Railways Act), the defendant is protected from liability. (e.g., If railway tracks legally laid near your house cause noise and vibrations, you cannot sue for nuisance).

core_concepts.title: Motive, Intention, and Malice
core_concepts.description:
General Rule: A lawful act does not become unlawful merely because it was done with a bad motive (malice). 
- Landmark Case: *Bradford Corporation v. Pickles* - Pickles maliciously stopped the flow of water on his land to force the corporation to buy his land at a high price. The court held that since extracting water from his own land was a lawful right, his bad motive did not make it a tort.

important_entities.name: Scienti non fit injuria
important_entities.key_fact: Mere knowledge does not imply consent.
important_entities.significance: A critical limitation to *Volenti non fit injuria*. Merely knowing that a risk exists does not mean the plaintiff consented to suffer it. In *Smith v. Baker*, a worker knew his workplace was dangerous but kept working to earn a living; the court held that his knowledge of the risk did not amount to legal consent.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'A and B agree to a sword fight to the death. A kills B. Can B's heirs sue in tort?' Yes. The defense of *Volenti non fit injuria* ONLY applies to lawful acts. You cannot legally consent to an unlawful act (like murder or severe grievous hurt).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: V A I P S (Volenti, Act of God, Inevitable, Private Defense, Statutory Authority)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use VAIPS to recall the primary general shields available to a tortfeasor.

exam_strategy_tips: If a question involves a spectator getting hit by a cricket ball at a stadium, the immediate defense to look for in the options is **Volenti non fit injuria**.
